column2: By the time Shao Youlian had met Li Hongzhang and agreed that striking at Hu Xueyan would be their principal means of obstructing Zuo Zongtang, Hu had only just reached Jiangning. When he discussed his itinerary with Madam Luosi, she strongly urged him to visit Jiangning before Shanghai. He thought her reasoning sound. Her praise of Mi Benchang had made him realize how well Mi could handle unexpected situations, which simplified matters. In Nanjing he must attend upon Zuo and could not control his own movements. In Shanghai, Mi would attend upon him. Any unfinished business could be left to Mi, allowing him to come and go as he pleased without missing the important duty of presiding over his daughter's wedding. He wrote to Mi and Gu Yingchun while preparing his baggage, most of which consisted of local gifts. Jiangning had more expectant circuit intendants than anywhere else, giving rise to a joke that its “circuit men were as thick as hairs.” They might go a whole year without an assignment, yet still had to maintain the appearance of third-rank dignitaries. Struggling to do so, they awaited visits from friends holding lucrative posts, hoping for a little help. Hu had many acquaintances there and was the God of Wealth. Everyone must receive attention, in gifts or silver. The silver could be drawn from Fukang in Jiangning, but the Hangzhou gifts filled an entire boat. A small steamer specially sent by the Yangtze naval forces towed it and Hu's private passenger boat through Jiaxing and Suzhou to Jiangning. Meanwhile, Li secretly telegraphed Shao, the Shanghai circuit intendant, summoning him to Tianjin for an important personal discussion. As a local official, Shao could not leave his post without authorization, so Li explained that a separate telegram would come from the Zongli Yamen. Shao was to prepare and sail north as soon as its official instructions arrived. They reached Shanghai only after Hu had left Hangzhou. But the sea passage to Tianjin took just two days and a night; when Shao saw Li, Hu was still on his way.

The ministers responsible for the northern and southern maritime administrations were thus each summoning a trusted man, but for opposite purposes. Zuo favoured war. Besides actively preparing southern coastal defences, he fully supported Peng Yulin, the imperial commissioner supervising military affairs in Guangdong. Li, though unwilling openly to defy respectable public opinion, secretly used every means to remove the war party's support and weaken its power and prestige. His first target was Zhang Peilun, the Left Deputy Censor-in-Chief, chief strategist for Grand Secretary Li Hongzao, leader of the war party. Bringing Zhang under control would be like capturing the leader to subdue the band. In terms of suppressing the advocates of war, winning Zhang over dealt with the root; attacking Hu dealt with the branches.

Hu, who would bear the first blow, knew nothing of this. On reaching Jiangning, he went first to rest at his own residence. He kept houses in the great cities but rarely visited them even once a year. Because of Zuo, this was his second stay at Jiangning that year. The “mistress” of this house was surnamed Wang. She had formerly run a brothel in Diaoyu Lane in Qinhuai's Old Quarter, but misfortune had struck her two adopted daughters in succession: one died for love, and the other eloped. The elopement could be left alone, but the death involved Madam Wang in a homicide case. She was finally acquitted and released, yet so disheartened that she no longer wished to earn her living by that precarious trade. The only alternative was to leave it and marry. Like Li Xiangjun's adoptive mother in Miscellaneous Records of Banqiao, she was a madam without being old, only a little over thirty and still attractive. There were men willing to offer riches for her. But Qinhuai courtesans inherited the Old Quarter's traditions from the late Ming and early Qing. They cared about refinement in food and daily life and admired poets and cultivated men. Those who wanted her had fortunes but no trace of elegance; those she wanted were gentle and refined but poor. She wished to leave the profession, yet could find no one to entrust her future to.

That was three years earlier. Jiangning Fukang had just acquired a new manager, Jiang Deyuan, transferred from another Fukang establishment. Well versed in the world of pleasure, he heard of her and hired her to manage Hu's residence. Normally it entertained especially important clients; when the proprietor visited, she became its hostess, presiding over the household. Those duties naturally extended to the bedroom. Comfortable living and freedom from restraint made her readily accept. When Hu came that autumn, the first thing to attract him was the pair of tiny curved feet beneath her skirt, slender as crescent moons. After a night together, he found Yuan Zicai's saying true: “A mature woman's charms surpass those of youth.” Besides generous gifts, he gave her the name Mother Wang Jiu, after the brothel keeper in the famous Southern Song tale set on West Lake, The Oil Vendor Wins the Flower Queen. Now, warned by Jiang, she had prepared Hu's favourite food and gathered plenty of news to entertain him.

Naturally, Hu cared most about news of Zuo. He was said to be increasingly old and infirm, but more overbearing than ever. Visitors and subordinates must never mention the western campaign: it opened a floodgate of talk about his achievements, his combination of kindness and authority in handling generals, and the miraculous unpredictability of his strategy. Then came the abuse, first of Zeng Guofan, next of Li Hongzhang, and sometimes of Shen Baozhen too. All three had preceded him in office, and many of their former subordinates remained in Jiangning, especially Zeng's. Whatever might be said of Li, people resented attacks on Zeng's character. Zeng's old followers often complained openly: “The present commander has grievances against the old commander. The rights and wrongs between them are hard to judge. Even if the old commander was at fault, he is dead and cannot hear the abuse. Why must we endure it? Besides, the arguments are neither just nor convincing. It all comes down to the same thing: he monopolized military funds and protected Ninth Marshal. We have heard it until our ears have grown calluses.” Hu wondered how Zuo could have declined so much in the mere six months since they last met. He was doubtful until Jiang confirmed it. “Many things cannot be done in Jiangning now. His Excellency begins with a lecture, then starts abusing people, talking without pause. When the allotted time is nearly over, a guard puts a teacup into his hand and someone outside immediately calls, ‘See the guest out!’ There is no chance to discuss business.”

“Surely that happens only occasionally?” “Almost every day. He becomes more excited with a larger audience. You needn't stand on ceremony, sir. Instead of attending a formal audience, go now and see him in the garden reception room or his office. Then you might discuss something useful.” Governors-general and governors generally received the provincial treasurer and judicial commissioner, together with circuit intendants and lesser subordinates, about once every five days, often on dates ending in three or eight. These formal visits, called “going up to the court,” took place in the official reception hall. Hu had arrived on the seventeenth of the tenth lunar month and intended to attend on the eighteenth. Accepting Jiang's advice, he instead put on his official robes at once and went straight by sedan chair to the Liangjiang governor-general's gates.

Seeing the God of Wealth, the gatekeepers were exceptionally attentive. On their own authority they opened the main gate and let his sedan be carried to the eaves of the reception hall. Word was sent inside, and instructions came back: “Ask His Excellency Hu to change into informal clothes. We shall meet in the office.” His attendant opened the clothes bundle, and Hu changed in the hall before being shown into the office, where Zuo was already waiting. Hu naturally made his full ceremonial greeting. Zuo helped him up himself and led him to the guest seats, where they exchanged the usual courtesies. As they spoke, Hu studied his eyes. A white film covered the left, while the right watered badly in a draught, forcing him to wipe it repeatedly with a silk handkerchief. Finding an opening, Hu said, “I heard your eyes were troubling you and had a special medicine prepared. It is cooling and clears the sight, with very good results.” Undoing a small brocade bundle he had brought, he added, “I also had a medicinal paste made for you. If it agrees with you, have your correspondence secretary write, and I shall send more.” “Thank you! Nowadays I depend on a few friends for help, not just with private matters; even official business must trouble you. When Shandong suffered floods, Liangjiang was assigned four hundred thousand taels for relief, and the provincial treasury could provide only half. Your generous help saved us. But Liangjiang still cannot repay you.” “Please don't mention it.” Hu nearly added that, with public funds deposited with him, he ought to be of service, but checked the words before speaking.

“With the situation in Vietnam urgent, the court has ordered Peng Xueqin to supervise military affairs in Guangdong. We have been friends for thirty years, and I must help him. Moreover, I have been commanded to prepare southern maritime defences. The waters off Guangdong and Fujian fall within my jurisdiction; I cannot neglect them. What infuriates me is that, since Zeng of Xiangxiang's time, officialdom in Liangjiang has grown steadily worse. Evasion and delay, with no thought for the wider situation—so once again I must rely on old friends.” Hu assented gravely. “Wang Langqing has left Beijing for Hunan to recruit six thousand men. He will need at least four thousand rifles. Li Shaoquan's elder brother-in-law has made a complete mess of the Jiangning Arsenal. If we order the Shanghai Manufacturing Bureau to produce them, first the money is not yet available, and second they cannot arrive in time for the emergency. So I thought the Transport Bureau might find a way. What do you say, Xueyan?” “I don't yet know the exact number of Western rifles in stock. But if you require four thousand, I shall find some means of supplying the full number.” “Good! I knew that a word to you would settle it. Nothing could be more satisfying.” Referring to himself respectfully by his personal name, Hu replied, “Guangyong owes everything to your patronage. I dare not fail to serve you with all my heart and strength.”

“You are too modest. There is something else. The Ministry of Revenue will of course arrange pay and provisions for Wang's recruits, but the cost of mobilizing them is considerable. Liangjiang must contribute what it can. Could you help us once more?” In the past, Hu would simply have asked how much. Circumstances were different now. After a little thought, he replied, “Your Excellency, money is desperately tight in the market. Even if it were not, you must consider your old subordinate. If I raise whatever you ask now and later cannot supply Shaanxi and Gansu, I shall be like a man who jumps into a well to rescue someone.” The old subordinate was Liu Jintang. Hu held a commission with the western expedition's Transport Bureau, and his responsibilities had an order of priority. Raising funds for Liangjiang was additional work, which he could undertake if he had capacity to spare. Otherwise, the western army must come first. Zuo understood and could not disregard the concern. “Very well. Tomorrow I shall speak to the provincial treasurer again. If there really is difficulty, we shall have to rely on you to come to our rescue.” “You are too kind. When should I return for instructions?” By instructions, Hu meant the answer. “Soon. There will be news within two or three days.” Hu rose. “I shall act as you direct. For today, I take my leave.” “Are you free this evening?” Realizing that Zuo meant to invite him to dinner, Hu quickly said that he had an engagement he could not miss. “Then I won't keep you. I know you are busy. There is no need to call again. When there is news, I shall send for you.”

After his farewell salute, Hu went to a banquet in a riverside house on the Qinhuai. The guests were prominent men in Jiangning officialdom, unusually well informed, and he learned much inside news. Li Hongzhang was said to have formally told the Zongli Yamen that China's strength was insufficient and the Vietnamese affair must be settled promptly: there was no other satisfactory course. The Yamen, however, favoured notifying the countries of the world of France's coercion and unreasonable demands, making clear that the fault lay with France. If French troops attacked, China should fight. Li disagreed, but even if he wanted negotiations, he had no one to negotiate with: the French special envoy Tricou had left for Japan. “China's difficulty is that we want peace but dare not make it, and want war but cannot fight it,” said Zhang Fengchi, an expectant circuit intendant serving as foreign-affairs commissioner at the governor-general's headquarters. “Now each side is trying to outlast the other. The question is which can do it.” “Who do you think will last longer, Mr Feng?” “Hard to say. In France, only the foreign minister was initially so intransigent, but opinion has now become united. Their premier told parliament that they were determined to fight to the end in Vietnam. Meanwhile, our court's two great pillars may not be fire and water, but they are certainly pulling in opposite directions and cannot agree. That is deeply worrying.” The two pillars were plainly Li and Zuo. Most guests were Liangjiang officials, but many had close ties to Li. Their quarrel was a dangerous topic: an incautious word could bring trouble. Everyone remained silent.

Everyone, that is, except one man. Yugui, an expectant circuit intendant in Shandong, was a Mongol Bannerman. He had formerly awaited appointment in Liangjiang, acted in an established circuit post and held many assignments. Senior in service and the oldest man present, he was called Brother Yu by everyone. Clear-minded and ready to shoulder responsibility, he should have risen as an able official, but his blunt speech had harmed his prospects. The Shandong governor had sent him to consult Zuo about dredging the Grand Canal. He had spent half a month in Jiangning without getting anywhere, leaving him full of grievances. At mention of the quarrel, he could not remain silent. “Lords Zuo and Li have illustrious achievements and the admiration of the empire. The court has rewarded them with titles and high office. Their past military services are past; there is no need to keep discussing them. A true hero doesn't boast of former valour. Why do it?” He plainly meant Zuo. With the great official so near at hand, the subject became more perilous still, and nobody dared say a word. Slightly tipsy, Yugui took their silence as approval and grew more animated. “In war, speed is everything. If we talk emptily all day and neglect real work, what happens when the enemy reaches the city walls while we are still boasting that the spring wind has already passed the Jade Gate? Think what a state we shall be in!” The guests exchanged frightened looks. His closer friends were particularly worried. If this reached Zuo, Yugui would certainly be summoned. A severe scolding would be the least of it. What if Zuo asked, “What troops do you mean at the city walls? The French?” In anger, he could impeach Yugui by name for alarming the public and undermining civilian and military morale. Dismissal would be the minimum punishment. Someone hurriedly changed the subject. “Brother Yu, tonight let us discuss only pleasant things. Drink, drink!”

Yugui wanted to continue, but their host, Zhang Fengchi, seized his opportunity. “Brother Yu's black-faced roles ring like great bells and will sober us up. Come, give us a passage to delight our ears.” Others agreed enthusiastically. “His singing is wonderfully stirring. Quickly, where are the musicians?” String and wind players and percussionists were all available and soon took their places. When they asked what to play, Zhang said, “His specialities are Exploring Mount Yin and Ascending the Heavenly Terrace. Let us ascend the terrace first, then explore the mountain.” “No,” Yugui replied. “I shall change roles today and sing a bearded character. Give me Executing Ma Su.” The drummer struck up and the fiddle began. As the introductory music ended, Yugui changed his mind. “Better make it Ascending the Heavenly Terrace after all.” He had improvised some words to attack Zuo through the example of the Shu general who lost Jieting: “His words outrun his deeds; he will never be of great use.” But he reconsidered. He was a visitor here, and Zuo was, after all, an elderly man of high standing. Excessive insolence would be improper; he had better not go too far. Watching all this, Hu was deeply affected. He remembered Zuo in his vigorous prime, when even Zeng Guofan had to yield to him. Who could have imagined such decline in old age, and such contempt from others? Grieving for Zuo, he also began thinking of withdrawing while the current still ran strong.

He had been in Jiangning ten days, yet Zuo had not sent for him. Given the earlier instruction, he could hardly seek another audience. He asked acquaintances to inquire, but learned nothing definite. At last the summons came. This time Zuo wasted no words. “Xueyan, I have made other arrangements for Shaanxi and Gansu. Allocate two hundred and fifty thousand from the Transport Bureau's public funds.” The money was plainly for Wang Debang. It was an order, with no discussion, and Hu could only assent. “Can it be paid here?” “Wherever you wish.” “Good. Here, then. Open an account for Wang Langqing and issue him a passbook.” “Yes.” “When will you leave?” “I have been awaiting your instructions. Now that they are settled, I hope to leave tomorrow.” “Yes, you must return for the wedding. I have already told them to prepare a congratulatory letter for your daughter's marriage. We have shared hardships; I feel sorry that I cannot attend the feast.” “You are too kind.” “I should like to send something distinctive as well. What would you suggest? Don't stand on ceremony.” Hu thought for a moment. “A pair of wedding couplets in your own hand would truly bring glory to our humble house.” “A small matter. There is no time today, but I shall certainly send them before the wedding.” “You are so busy with public affairs that I am asking more than I should. Since you have granted the request, I shall reserve the place of honour in the wedding hall.”

This was an indirect way of making the promise binding. Zuo could not fail to keep his word, leaving two blank spaces in the place of honour. Understanding, he called for an attendant. An answer rang from the corridor, and an officer wearing a bright blue finial entered to await his orders. “I have promised His Excellency Hu a pair of couplets for his daughter's wedding. Whenever you see me with a little time to spare, remind me, so that I don't fail in courtesy. Keep reminding me.” “Yes.” “Good. That settles it.” He asked Hu, “You are going to Shanghai first?” “Yes.” “Is there anything you need me to arrange?” Hu was uneasy about the foreign loan principal soon falling due. But Mi had sent no letter, so he supposed everything had been settled. There was no need to trouble Zuo. “I shall ask when something arises.” “Very well. I have not even found time to give you a dinner on this visit. It is hardly proper.” “You are too courteous. Is there anything you would like me to attend to in Shanghai or Hangzhou?” Zuo thought briefly. “Only those four thousand rifles for Wang Langqing.” “I shall certainly settle that.” “Nothing else. As you said yourself, I shall ask when something comes to mind.” Hu took his leave, then earnestly reminded the attendant officers that they must prompt Zuo about the couplets. Naturally, he also presented a red envelope marked “Parting Gift.”

As soon as he reached Shanghai, Hu regretted the time wasted in Jiangning. The city seemed transformed. Business was depressed. Acquaintances, on meeting, asked either for war news or where it would be safest to take refuge. Nothing of the sort had been apparent in Jiangning. Such conditions were a banker's greatest fear: rumours everywhere and people in panic. The wealthy believed cash in hand was safest, so deposits were withdrawn but not replaced. Several banks had already failed through lack of funds to meet payments. Fukang's excellent name protected it to some extent, but another danger was developing in secret. Mi kept his lips sealed and let Hu know nothing. Even what Hu could see was enough to cause a severe headache. First came Wang Debang's four thousand rifles. The Transport Bureau had only twenty-five hundred in stock, leaving fifteen hundred to buy. At eighteen taels of standard silver each, with freight, they would cost about thirty thousand taels. That was relatively minor. The trouble was that Hu had given Zuo an unqualified promise. Failure to deliver the full number would affect his credit. “You needn't attach too much importance to it, Little Uncle,” Gu said. “You can show Zuo of Xiangyin the order later.” “Yingchun, I have never fallen short of my word to him. This may be one of the last one or two commissions I carry out for him. What matters most is how one finishes. If I break my word at the end, he may suspect that, no longer needing his protection, I am less loyal. Besides, I cannot bear to destroy a name built over so many years for such a small matter. Think of something. You must help me.” Gu had always handled arms purchases, and no such appeal had ever been necessary. The sudden plea made him uncomfortable. After considering for some time, he said, “Let us see whether Japan offers a way. If there is stock ready, we can still make the deadline. But we shall not be able to bargain over the price.” “Price is a small matter. Speed is everything. Start today.”

After two days' work, Gu at last had a lead. Eager to tell Hu, he looked everywhere but could not find him. Late that night, just as Gu was about to retire, Hu arrived unannounced, looking unwell. Ruixiang attended to him herself, bringing ginseng broth. “You must be exhausted, Master. Are you hungry?” “Hungry, yes, but I can't eat.” “Think of something appetizing for supper,” Gu told her. When she had gone, Hu asked, “Has Seventh Sister gone to bed?” “Yes. She retires early.” “Then don't disturb her. I hear you have been looking for me all day.” Gu brightened. “I have good news. We have found the rifles.” “Excellent! Where?” “Japan. Interestingly, they were originally intended for the French.” “Better still. How did it happen?” The French had hurriedly sent reinforcements and wanted to obtain additional rifles locally in the East. They had found a Japanese arms dealer with two thousand for sale. Through extensive inquiries, Gu learned of the stock and had a telegram sent offering a high price for fifteen hundred. The reply asked twenty-five taels each, plus freight. “Has the bargain been settled?” “Yes, at his price, with freight for our account. Ten thousand taels have already been telegraphed to him. Delivery in Shanghai in half a month.”

“Twenty-five it is. At least that is one worry settled.” Hu suddenly asked, “Have you heard that Old Mi is secretly trading in goods from north and south without telling me?” Gu hesitated. “I have heard something, but know no details.” “They say a ship struck a French mine and sank, with a considerable loss.” “The loss can't be large. There would certainly be insurance.” Hu nodded, reassured. “Do you think I should confront him?” The matter was important, and Gu dared not answer hastily. After a long pause, he asked instead, “What do you think?” “As long as the risk isn't great, I think it better to say nothing. As the saying goes, ‘Once you have gone astray, you may as well tear down the cowshed.’ If I expose it, he may simply throw off all restraint and do business on a large scale. Then I shall have to replace him. The difficulty is finding anyone suitable.”

Hu then spoke of another worry. The second repayment of principal on the foreign loan fell due at the end of the tenth lunar month. Since the beginning of that month, Mi had repeatedly asked at the Shanghai circuit intendant's office, only to be told that the provinces had not yet remitted the money. When Hu arrived and called on Shao Youlian, he received the same answer, with one addition: “Don't worry. I shall press them as hard as I can. The money should all be in around the due date.” “It must be before the deadline, not after. You know how particular foreigners are about keeping faith.” “I know. But the money is not in my hands. What can I do? Mr Hu, five hundred thousand taels is nothing to you. If it hasn't all arrived before the deadline, advance it yourself. You will only lose a few days' interest.” That silenced Hu. “He wasn't wrong. Normally an advance would be nothing. Who could have known that this time I couldn't make it? Misfortunes have happened to coincide, and I cannot explain my difficulty.”

Gu had to think for a moment to understand Hu's phrase: several unlucky circumstances coming together made a coincidence of misfortunes. There were many. First, business was poor and money desperately tight. Second, Hu knew that his stocks of silk and cocoons had trapped him and had tried hard to escape. Yet through one mishap after another, his scheme to acquire modern silk-reeling factories and create an outlet for the stock had never succeeded. Silk remained in both Tianjin and Shanghai, without buyers even at reduced prices. Third, Zuo had already borrowed two hundred thousand taels for relief contributions and now required another two hundred and fifty thousand for Wang Debang. Although these were the Transport Bureau's public funds, their removal still reduced the cash available for Hu to deploy. Fourth, the wedding on the fifth of the eleventh month was approaching. Such a grand occasion meant heavy spending; at least another two hundred thousand taels must be ready. Finally, Mi was privately using customers' names to withdraw deposits for his trade in northern and southern goods. Gu estimated the amount at roughly a hundred thousand taels. “Today is the twenty-fifth of the tenth month,” Hu said. “This month has only twenty-nine days. There are fewer than ten days until the fifth of next month. How can I attend to the wedding with an easy mind until I have put our cash position in order?” “Don't be too anxious. After all, it is only five hundred thousand. And it isn't your personal debt. There must be a solution.” “Then we must look for it early.”

After some thought, Gu said, “We can only proceed step by step. Press the Shanghai circuit intendant while making our own arrangements to mobilize funds. If neither succeeds, there is a final course: ask HSBC for an extension. At worst, we pay extra interest.” “I thought of that too. But what if they say, like Shao Xiaocun, ‘Why don't you advance it yourself?’ I shall have no answer.” “They won't. Foreigners distinguish public from private affairs. They won't expect a private person to advance money for a public debt. If they do say so, tell them, ‘Better for you to advance it than for me to do it. Before, HSBC wanted to lend to Fukang. Fukang didn't want the money but eventually took it. Let this again count as a loan from HSBC to Fukang.’ See what they say.” Hu nodded earnestly. “That is true.” “If you agree, I can settle it with HSBC in advance. Then you can put your mind at rest.” “Not so fast!” Hu repeatedly waved his hand. He had his own concerns. Requesting an extension would amount to admitting that he could not even advance five hundred thousand taels. If that became known, it would damage his golden reputation. Zuo would doubt his resources and ability, and on the fifth of the next month the crowds of wedding guests would be bound to discuss it. The glory of the celebration would be greatly diminished.

“Let us take the first and second steps for now,” Hu said. “I shall handle the first and entrust the second to you.” The first meant pressing the circuit intendant's office; the second, finding ways to arrange funds themselves. In practice, that meant urging Mi to act. Because of their earlier friction, Gu was unwilling to undertake an arduous, thankless task that might achieve nothing. His face showed his reluctance. “What is it?” “I should like us to exchange roles. Leave the first step to me, and take the second yourself. You have every right to press Old Mi. If I do it, he will resent it and pay no attention.” “Very well. But we must act quickly.” “I shall go first thing tomorrow. I have acquaintances at the office. Come for lunch and hear the news.” “Good. These next few days we must see each other morning and evening.”
